title: Hiram
dek: A miller and Elder whose business rescue is rejected, whose distrust of adventurers sometimes gives way to cooperation, and whose civic work includes local defense.

body:
Hiram is a Pristinian miller and Elder who brings business interests, pride and sharp suspicion of adventurers into the town’s public decisions. He can argue for a financial rescue that favors his own circle, defend Magda’s years of service and help prepare ordinary residents for danger. His disagreements with Kaja and Melian belong to that history.

Continuity and office

Hiram appears among Pristinia’s Elders. In the early assembly he opposes repeated selection, arguing that an Elder should be able to concentrate on the settlement instead of popularity. That is his argument about an institutional design, not a description of every later rule.

The debt crisis

He warns that Pristinia’s resources cannot meet its obligations to the Rahu, distinguishing recurring shortfalls from total debt. He presents default as a threat to war and trust, then turns to Ziegler’s proposed solution. Kaja’s resistance and Magda’s announced decision preserve the debate rather than making Hiram’s preferred answer inevitable.

Local defense

In a later public assembly Hiram reports roughly two dozen volunteers meeting at the Archery Range on a schedule he calls “biweekly”, with basic equipment and mainly defensive capabilities. The report records local training at that moment; it is not a permanent troop count or a claim that he created the range.

Recorded scenes

  • Hiram seated among the Elders
  • His argument against repeated selection
  • Debt and the prospect of default
  • Turning to Ziegler’s proposal
  • Reporting the volunteers’ training

The miller behind the office

The early assembly describes a sun-tanned man with rolled sleeves and callused hands. Later, when asked what he contributes, Hiram indignantly identifies his mill: the wheat of Pristinia’s fields becomes flour there. He says he has made arrangements for continued supply and has even paid farmers to leave land unsown so it can recover, though paying people not to work plainly irritates him.

His confidence in himself can be comic and self-serving. Introducing a solution to the debt crisis, he calls himself Pristinia’s youngest-ever Elder and credits his own foresight. That is how he presents himself, rather than an independently verified record of the town’s entire electoral past.

His solution is not the council’s decision

Hiram’s preferred rescue comes through Ziegler and a company controlled by the businesspeople supplying its capital, including himself. He argues that refusing taxes has allowed businesses to flourish enough to help the town. Kaja instead favors income-based taxation and resists concentrated control.

He leaves the discussion with Magda, asking for tea and her favorite biscuits. When the Elders return, Magda is supported by Kaja and announces that the offer has been declined by a split decision. Hiram enters scowling and later glowers at the table. The visible outcome defeats the solution he introduced; the account does not turn his stake in the proposal into proof of undisclosed criminal conduct.

Resentment, accommodation and an embarrassing question

At a festival Hiram drunkenly accuses adventurers of enjoying themselves while thefts threaten the town and presses them to donate a bounty if they catch the culprits. In a later governance discussion he worries that a separate adventurer council will weaken the Elders, demands that visitors provide their own housing and reacts with surprise when Fenwick offers to discuss payment. His resentment does not prevent every practical concession.

The same meeting exposes his inattention. He asks for a captured child to be brought before the Elders, only to be told that the child is already in Pristinia’s custody. He says he has had other business; the narrator marks his embarrassment, and he stops speaking. The scene preserves an official claiming the right to be involved while failing to keep up with the matter before him.

Care, candidacy and practical defense

When Magda’s difficulty with the work becomes apparent, Hiram says she has served for nearly his whole adult life and has earned the right to decide when and how to step down. He helps Kaja and Katherine take her home. This is his tribute and practical help, not a confirmed retirement.

During the Rahu war he participates in discussion of supplies and the burial of the dead. He favors burning enemy bodies, but also warns against adopting enemy tactics without considering the town’s reputation. Later Hawthorne names him and Kaja as candidates who have given up their seats for a full election. Hiram questions an arrangement under which a person could run but not vote; his later participation does not itself identify that election’s winners.

At the later law assembly he can report the volunteers’ training and the occasional use of the jail. Those concrete answers sit alongside his earlier lapses. His latest checked quest appearance here is at that assembly, on 17, Month of Namo’o · Year 3; a later term of office is not established by this selection.
